opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it really depends on what you want to do. If your goal is to work in industry, especially as an engineer at a place doing frontier AI, the most valuable thing is your ability to actually build things: write solid code, debug large systems, ship quickly, and work well with other people. A PhD trains some of that, but a lot of it is optimized for something else: publishing papers, finding a narrow problem, and defending a novel idea to reviewers.

In industry, especially now, research and engineering have kind of merged. The bottleneck is often not "do you have a clever idea?" but "can you make this thing work at scale, reliably, and fast?" Many of the people I respect most are extremely strong engineers who understand the research deeply, and you don't need a PhD to get there. You can learn a lot by just doing: contributing to open source, building your own projects, joining a good team early and learning from people who are better than you.

There's also the opportunity cost. A PhD is five or six years. In a field moving this fast, five years is a whole era. If you spend that time in industry working on real systems with real compute, you might grow much faster and have much more impact.

That said, I don't think a PhD is useless. If you really love open-ended research, want academic freedom, or want to become a professor, it makes total sense. But if you're doing it just because it seems like the default path or a credential you need for an industry job, I'd say think twice. What companies care about more and more is what you've actually built and whether you can make things work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I want to be careful with the framing, because I don't think a PhD is useless. I think it's unnecessary for most industry careers, and people treat it as a requirement when it isn't.

My own path shaped this view. I was doing research in grad school, building things like Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, and what actually opened doors for me was the code. People at companies found the project, used it, and that led to conversations. Nobody asked me whether I had finished a dissertation. They asked whether I could ship a system that other people could rely on.

The core issue is what a PhD optimizes for. A PhD trains you to find a narrow question, go very deep, and produce novel results that survive peer review. That's a real skill. But most industry work, even at AI labs, is about engineering: making things work at scale, debugging distributed training runs, making an API reliable, understanding tradeoffs under deadlines. Those skills are learned by doing, and you can start doing them at twenty-two instead of twenty-eight.

There's also an opportunity cost that people underestimate. Five or six years is a long time in a field that changes every eighteen months. Someone who joins a strong team right after a master's degree spends those years working on real problems with real compute and real users. By the time their peer finishes a PhD, they often have more relevant experience and more impact, and they've been paid for it.

Now, the honest caveat. If you want to lead a research direction, define new problems, or work in a role where publishing is the job, the PhD still matters a lot, and some teams filter hard on it. And the PhD gives you a protected space to think slowly, which industry rarely does. So if you genuinely love research as a way of life, do it.

But if your goal is to build things in industry, my advice is simple: build something people use, put it in public, and let the work speak. That has a much higher hit rate than a credential.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t say a PhD is unnecessary for every industry career. It really depends on the work you want to do. If you want to become a research scientist, that training can be valuable, and some roles require it. But if your goal is to build products or solve practical business problems, a PhD isn’t necessarily the most direct path.

You can learn a lot by working on real problems, getting feedback, and taking responsibility for what you build. A PhD is a substantial commitment, so I’d start with the question: do you actually enjoy research? If you do, it can be a great choice. If you’re doing it mainly because you think you need another credential to succeed in industry, I’d question that assumption.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say a PhD is unnecessary for every industry career. It depends on the work you want to do. If you want to pursue specialized research, a PhD can be valuable, and some roles require one. But if your goal is to build products or solve practical engineering problems, you can often develop those skills by working directly in industry.

A PhD takes several years, so there’s an opportunity cost. During that time, you could be gaining experience, learning from colleagues, and figuring out what problems you actually enjoy solving. I think the question is whether the training a PhD provides is necessary for the kind of work you want to do. If it is, that’s a good reason to pursue one. If it isn’t, there are other paths.
